1.open: Who is someone who encouraged you when you were just starting something new, and what did they say or do?
questions: Paul says he remembers their "work of faith," their "labor of love," and their "enduring hope" (v. 3). Which of these three do you see most in your own life right now, and which feels thinnest?
Paul calls them "beloved by God" before he says anything else about them (v. 4). Why might it matter that he starts there? How easy is it for you to believe that about yourself?
Paul says the gospel came "not only in word, but also in power, in the Holy Spirit, and with great conviction" (v. 5). What do you think that looked like for the people who first heard it?
Paul also says, "you know we lived among you for your sake" (v. 5). Whose life has made the message about Jesus believable to you, and what did they do?

They welcomed the message "with the joy of the Holy Spirit, in spite of your great suffering" (v. 6). How can joy and hard times sit side by side? Where have you seen that, or where does it feel hard to believe?
Verse 9 says they turned "from idols to serve the living and true God." What are the modern things people serve or lean on in place of God, and what might turning away from them cost?
They also waited "to await His Son from heaven" (v. 10). How does looking ahead to Jesus' return change the way you face a hard week? If it does not change much for you, what gets in the way?
Verse 4 says God has chosen them, and Christians understand that in different ways. Whichever way you lean, what does it say to you about how God sees the people he calls?
1.life: Think of one person whose faith has encouraged you. This week, write or text them a short note like Paul's, telling them specifically what you see God doing in their life.
1.prayer: Thank God for the people who have shown you what faith looks like. Ask him to give your group faith that acts, love that works hard, and hope that lasts.
1.tip: Verse 4 and the word "chosen" can pull the group into a long debate. Say in one line that Christians read it differently, then bring the focus back to Paul's main point: these believers were loved, and their lives showed it. Also leave room for anyone who feels their own faith is small.

2.open: Think of a teacher, coach or friend who made a real difference in your life. What did they do that showed they cared about you and not just the job?
questions: Paul says they had suffered "shameful treatment in Philippi," yet they were "bold in our God" to speak in Thessalonica (v. 2). What do you think gave them that courage?
Paul says their appeal did not come from "deceit or ulterior motives or trickery" (v. 3). Why do you think he spends so much time on his motives? What makes a person's motives easy or hard to trust?

In verses 7 and 8 Paul compares himself to "a nursing mother caring for her children," and says they shared "our own lives as well." What does it look like today to share your life with someone and not just your opinions?
Paul says "we worked night and day so that we would not be a burden to anyone" (v. 9). Where have you seen someone give up comfort or convenience so that others could hear good news freely?
In verse 12 Paul describes encouraging, comforting and urging, like a father. Which of those three do you most need right now, and which do you find easiest to give?

Verse 13 says they received the message "not as the word of men, but as it truly is, the word of God." How would you describe, honestly, how the Bible feels to you right now: alive, distant, confusing, or something else?
The believers in Thessalonica were suffering from their own neighbors (v. 14). What does faith cost people you know, even in small ways, and how can we stand beside them?
In verses 19 and 20 Paul calls the believers "our hope, our joy, our crown of boasting." Who are the people you feel that way about, and have you told them?
2.life: Pick one person this week and give them more than advice. Share some of your time, a meal, or your own story. Afterward, notice how Paul's picture of a caring mother and father shaped what you did.
2.prayer: Thank God for the people who shared more than words with you. Ask for a heart like Paul's, honest in motive and gentle in love, toward the people God puts in your path.
2.tip: Verses 14 to 16 are sharp, and they have been used to hurt Jewish people. Christians read them differently: some hear angry words about particular opponents, some think they were a verdict on a whole people, and some think a later hand added them. Say plainly that Paul was Jewish himself and that most churches firmly reject blaming all Jews. Then bring the group back to the rest of the chapter.

3.open: Think of a time you waited anxiously to hear news about someone you cared about. How did you handle the waiting?
questions: Paul says, "when we could bear it no longer," he sent Timothy (v. 1). Why do you think Paul was so worried about people he had known for such a short time?

Paul had warned them that "we would suffer persecution" and it "has come to pass" (v. 4). Why might it help new believers to hear that hard times are expected and not a sign that something has gone wrong?
Paul feared "that the tempter had somehow tempted you and that our labor might have been in vain" (v. 5). What kinds of pressure make it hard to keep trusting God today?
Timothy returned with "good news about your faith, your love" (v. 6). What does it tell you that Paul cared about their love as much as their belief?

Paul says, "now we can go on living, as long as you are standing firm in the Lord" (v. 8). What do you make of how deeply he is tied to these people? Who in your life are you that tied to, or wish you were?
Paul asks, "How can we adequately thank God for you" (v. 9). Who has God used to encourage your faith, and have they ever heard you say so?
Paul prays that the Lord would cause them to "increase and overflow with love for one another and for everyone else" (v. 12). Where is it hardest for you to love beyond your own circle?

Paul worries about people who are far away and about faith that is still growing. If you are in a season of doubt or feeling worn thin, what would you want someone like Timothy to say to you, or to hear from you?
3.life: Pick one person who is far away or going through something hard. Send them a real message this week, a call, a note or a text, telling them you are thinking of them and praying for them.
3.prayer: Thank God for the people who have steadied your faith. Pray by name for someone who is struggling, and ask that their love and trust would grow.
3.tip: Paul's strong feelings in verses 1 to 10 can make some people feel their own faith should be more intense, while others may feel they have no one like Timothy. Keep the focus on ordinary encouragement, and gently make space for anyone who feels alone, since the group itself can be that encouragement. Verse 13 mentions Jesus coming "with all His saints," and interpreters differ on who that means, so mention it briefly and move on.

4.open: Who is someone you could always count on to show up when life got hard, and what did they do?
questions: Paul says the church already lives the way he taught, yet he asks them to do so "all the more" (v. 1). Why is it easy to stop growing once we think we are doing fine?
Paul says, "it is God's will that you should be holy" (v. 3). When you hear the word holy, what comes to mind, and how does it compare with what Paul describes in this passage?

Paul writes to people living among neighbors who saw sexual behavior very differently from the church (v. 5). What pressures do people today face in this area, and how can a church talk about it without shame or judgment?
Verse 4 can be read as controlling your own body or living honorably with your own wife, and translations differ. Why might it matter that Paul cares about both honor and respect for others (v. 6)?

Paul says God "has not called us to impurity, but to holiness" (v. 7), and gives his Holy Spirit to those who follow him (v. 8). How does it change things to see holiness as help from God and not only a list of rules?

Paul urges them "to aspire to live quietly, to attend to your own matters, and to work with your own hands" (v. 11). What would that look like in your week, and how might it shape how outsiders see your faith?

Paul does not want them to "grieve like the rest, who are without hope" (v. 13). Where have you seen grief and hope sit side by side, or where has hope felt hard to find? It is fine to answer honestly if hope feels thin right now.
Paul ends with "encourage one another with these words" (v. 18). Who needs that kind of encouragement from you, and what could you say or do?
4.life: Think of one person who is grieving or worn down. This week, reach out with a call, a visit or a meal, and share one of Paul's words of hope in your own plain language.
4.prayer: Thank God that Jesus died and rose again, and that those who have died trusting him are not lost. Ask for his help to live in love and holiness, and pray for anyone in the group who is grieving.
4.tip: Verses 3 to 8 on sexual ethics and verses 16 and 17 on the "rapture" can pull the whole evening off course. Name briefly that Christians read verses 16 and 17 differently, then point back to Paul's own aim in verse 18, which is comfort. For the sexual ethics section, keep the tone gentle and grace-first, since some in the room may carry real pain or shame, and do not press anyone to share.

5.open: Tell about a time something happened when you were not expecting it, good or bad. How did you react?
questions: Paul says the Day of the Lord "will come like a thief in the night" (v. 2). Why do you think he chose that picture, and how does it land with you: uneasy, curious, hopeful, or something else?
Paul tells the church, "you are all sons of the light and sons of the day" (v. 5). What do you think it looks like to live in the day instead of the night in ordinary life?
Verse 8 pictures "the breastplate of faith and love, and the helmet of our hope of salvation." Which of the three, faith, love or hope, feels strongest in you right now, and which feels thin?
Paul writes, "encourage and build one another up" (v. 11). Who has done that for you, and what did they actually say or do?

Verse 14 asks the church to "admonish the unruly, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with everyone." Which of these do you most need from others on a hard day, and which do you find easiest to give?
"Rejoice at all times" and "Give thanks in every circumstance" (vv. 16, 18) can sound impossible in a hard season. How do you hear those words when you do not feel joyful or thankful?
Paul says, "test all things. Hold fast to what is good" (v. 21). How do you sort out what to believe from sermons, friends, or social media?
Verse 24 says, "The One who calls you is faithful, and He will do it." Where do you want that to be true in your life, even if you are not sure it is?
5.life: Pick one person this week who could use a lift. Send a note, a text or a call that tells them something specific you value in them.
5.prayer: Thank God that he is faithful and finishes what he starts. Ask him to help each of you stay awake to his work and to build up the people close to you.
5.tip: Questions about the end times can take over the whole evening. Christians disagree on how verse 9 fits with the timing of Jesus' return, so say that plainly, don't try to settle it, and bring the group back to Paul's point: live alert and encourage one another.
